paragraphs: Sentence summarization compresses a sentence while preserving its central message. For applications such as headline generation, the amount of available space also matters: a useful summary must convey the gist within a length constraint. This paper focuses on explicitly controlling the number of characters, a requirement that previous work had given less attention than improving summarization scores.

The authors propose a dynamic programming algorithm built around Connectionist Temporal Classification, or CTC, for non-autoregressive sentence summarization. The central contribution is to make character length an explicit part of producing the summary. Counting characters addresses a different requirement from merely encouraging generally shorter text, because it connects the output to a concrete measure of its size.

The reported results show both higher ROUGE scores and more complete sentences. These findings matter together: the approach addresses length control while also improving the reported measures of summary quality. The work therefore presents explicit character budgeting as compatible with preserving content and sentence completeness in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2022-a-character-level-length-co.tldr: A CTC-based dynamic programming algorithm explicitly controls summary length in characters while improving reported ROUGE scores and sentence completeness.

paragraphs: Hashing represents data with compact codes, making the quality of those codes central to its usefulness. Many learning objectives have been designed heuristically to produce good codes, but the paper identifies a shortage of theoretical guidance about which characteristics support performance. It seeks a principled connection between the organization of hash codes and their eventual quality.

The authors prove that separation between classes and compactness within each class determine a lower bound on hash-code performance. In plain terms, codes should distinguish different classes while keeping members of the same class close together. Encouraging these properties could raise the bound. To pursue this objective, they introduce a surrogate model that estimates and controls the posterior distribution of hash codes, yielding low-bias optimization.

Experiments across a series of hash models report improvements for every model tested. The largest reported increases are 26.5% in mean Average Precision and 20.5% in accuracy. These are maximum observed gains, while the broader contribution is a theoretically motivated objective paired with a practical optimization method.
neurips-2022-a-lower-bound-of-hash-codes.tldr: The paper derives a performance lower bound from hash-code separation and compactness, then uses it to guide a method that improves tested hash models.

paragraphs: Stereo vision depends on matching corresponding regions in two images. Repetitive or nearly textureless surfaces make this difficult. Active stereo adds a projected pseudo-random pattern to make regions easier to distinguish, but that pattern also changes image appearance. The paper investigates whether this change disrupts deep learning methods developed for stereo matching.

The authors introduce the Active-Passive SimStereo dataset and a benchmark for comparing performance on images with and without active patterns. They also conduct an ablation study to examine which parts of stereo architectures respond poorly to the appearance change. This makes the investigation more specific than a comparison of final predictions alone.

Across twenty selected methods, feature extraction and matching modules generalize successfully to active stereo. However, disparity refinement is negatively affected in ACVNet, CascadeStereo, and StereoNet because those modules depend on input appearance. The findings locate a particular vulnerability within the tested architectures: the projected pattern can support matching while still interfering with later refinement.
neurips-2022-active-passive-simstereo-be.tldr: A new stereo benchmark finds that active patterns transfer well through tested feature and matching modules but harm refinement in three architectures.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained model to a new task can require substantial memory, even when the model already provides useful representations. A major contributor is the activation data saved during training for the backward computation. Back Razor targets this stored information so that transfer learning becomes less demanding without requiring changes to the network architecture.

Its key idea is asymmetric sparsification. Activations remain dense during the forward computation, but the versions retained for backpropagation are pruned. This preserves the precision of the forward calculation while reducing what must be kept in memory. The authors also analyze convergence and show that, under mild conditions, Back Razor retains a convergence rate similar to ordinary stochastic gradient descent.

Experiments cover convolutional networks and vision transformers across classification, dense prediction, and language modeling. The reported results include up to 97% sparsity and a 9.2-fold memory saving without accuracy loss. These findings support substantial memory reductions in the evaluated transfer settings, with the asymmetry between forward computation and backward storage providing the central mechanism.
neurips-2022-back-razor-memory-efficient.tldr: Back Razor reduces transfer-learning memory by pruning activations saved for backpropagation while keeping forward computation dense.

paragraphs: When data follows known differential equations, a statistical model can benefit from building those equations into its structure. This paper develops Gaussian processes whose realizations strictly obey a specified system of linear, homogeneous ordinary differential equations with constant coefficients. The equation class is an explicit part of the construction's scope.

The authors construct the covariance functions that define these processes using an algorithmic, symbolic method based on Smith normal form. Their approach removes two restrictions found in existing methods: certain requirements concerning uniqueness of solutions and the requirement that the system be controllable. This extends the systems that can be represented within the stated class of differential equations.

The resulting models, called LODE-GPs, use the equations as a strong inductive bias, improving modeling of data with that structure. Experiments demonstrate their effectiveness, including learning physically interpretable parameters by maximizing likelihood. The contribution connects exact equation compliance with statistical learning, allowing the prescribed dynamics to shape the model while parameters are learned from observations.
neurips-2022-constraining-gaussian-proce.tldr: LODE-GPs construct Gaussian-process covariances that enforce linear homogeneous differential equations while removing two restrictions of earlier approaches.

paragraphs: Spatio-temporal video grounding finds the object described by a text expression and follows its location through the relevant video frames. Treating this as a collection of separate frame-grounding problems can produce inconsistent language-image alignment and inconsistent predictions over time. The paper addresses both problems within a single end-to-end framework called STCAT.

STCAT introduces a multimodal template that serves as a shared objective across the video. This template constrains the region being located and connects predictions between frames. An encoder-decoder architecture models global video and text context to generate the template. Together, these components give individual frame predictions a common reference informed by the broader sequence.

The approach operates without relying on pretrained object detectors. Experiments on VidSTG and HC-STVG report clear improvements over previous leading methods. The findings support the value of explicitly connecting predictions across frames: identifying an object from language benefits from consistent interpretation throughout a video, alongside accurate localization in individual images.
neurips-2022-embracing-consistency-a-one.tldr: STCAT uses a shared video-text template to improve consistency when locating a described object across video frames.

paragraphs: This paper examines transformer attention through the lens of nonparametric kernel regression. In the authors' account, conventional dot-product attention corresponds to unnormalized Gaussian kernels under a Gaussian-mixture assumption about queries. Because that assumption need not hold in practice, they investigate a different family of kernels for relating queries and keys.

FourierFormer replaces dot-product kernels with generalized Fourier integral kernels. These kernels can automatically capture dependencies between data features, removing the need to tune a covariance matrix for that purpose. The authors also prove that their proposed kernels can efficiently approximate arbitrary key and query distributions. This provides theoretical support for a more flexible treatment of the distributions involved in attention.

Empirical evaluations include language modeling and image classification. Compared with the baseline dot-product transformers, FourierFormers achieve better accuracy and less redundancy between attention heads. The results connect the kernel-level change to both prediction quality and how distinctly the heads behave, supporting the proposed attention mechanism in the applications evaluated.
neurips-2022-fourierformer-transformer-m.tldr: FourierFormer replaces dot-product attention kernels with generalized Fourier kernels, improving reported accuracy and reducing attention-head redundancy.

paragraphs: Adapting a generative adversarial network to a target domain is useful when little training data is available. This paper reduces the number of parameters that must be optimized during that adaptation. Its domain-modulation technique represents the adjustment with a vector of six thousand values, instead of updating StyleGAN2's thirty million weights.

Applied to existing leading adaptation methods, the compact parameterization shows almost the same expressiveness as the full parameter space. The authors also introduce a regularization loss that substantially improves the diversity of the adapted generator. These contributions address both the size of the adaptation problem and the variety of outputs the resulting model produces.

The reduced parameter space also enables HyperDomainNet, a hypernetwork that predicts the modulation parameters for a requested target domain. This lets one model support multiple domains through its input query. Experiments show successful learning of several domains together and suggest possible generalization to unseen domains. That last result is presented as a possibility supported by empirical evidence.
neurips-2022-hyperdomainnet-universal-do.tldr: HyperDomainNet uses a compact generator-modulation vector to support GAN adaptation across multiple domains, with possible transfer to unseen ones.

paragraphs: Data augmentation creates variations of training examples to improve learning. For graphs, however, modifying nodes or edges can change the property that determines the graph's label. The authors conjecture that violations of the assumption that augmentation preserves labels may help explain why graph contrastive learning has not matched the promise seen in visual contrastive learning.

They propose augmenting graphs in representation space, where the model encodes their information, instead of directly modifying graph structure or extracting subgraphs. The method generates examples in the most challenging direction while preserving the original label. Its aim is to expose the learner to difficult variations without changing what the example is supposed to represent.

In semi-supervised graph classification, the approach outperforms classical graph neural network methods and recent graph contrastive methods on eight benchmarks. Additional experiments explore aspects of label-preserving augmentation. These results support the proposed representation-space method, while the explanation that label changes constrain existing approaches remains framed as the authors' motivating conjecture.
neurips-2022-label-invariant-augmentatio.tldr: The paper creates challenging, label-preserving augmentations in graph representation space and reports improved semi-supervised classification on eight benchmarks.

paragraphs: A point-cloud classifier can perform well on familiar data yet struggle when different acquisition procedures change the geometry it sees. This paper studies generalization from a source domain to an unseen target domain. Its starting observation is that local geometric structures transfer more readily than representations of an entire shape.

The proposed part-based domain generalization network, PDG, builds a common part-template feature space for source and target domains. It first organizes shapes into part-level features, then expresses those features through the shared templates. A dedicated aggregation module combines these aligned part representations into a shape representation. This gives differently acquired shapes a shared way to describe their constituent geometry.

The authors further apply contrastive learning to the part-based shape representations to improve robustness. Experiments and ablations on 3DDA and 3DDG benchmarks support the approach relative to previous leading methods. The findings suggest that aligning local parts can reduce the impact of geometry differences and improve classification when a model encounters an unfamiliar domain.
neurips-2022-learning-generalizable-part.tldr: PDG aligns point-cloud parts through shared templates to improve classification generalization across changes in data acquisition.

paragraphs: Non-rigid shape matching seeks correspondences between shapes that may be deformed. Functional-map methods depend strongly on a spectral-resolution setting, whose choice can affect accuracy or cause overfitting. This paper reduces the burden of selecting one resolution by learning how to combine correspondence information computed at several resolutions.

The framework constructs multiple functional maps, each characterizing correspondence at a different spectral resolution. A spectral attention network combines these into one coherent final correspondence. The network can be trained to adapt its use of resolution to the input shapes, and the framework supports both supervised and unsupervised learning. Resolution thus becomes something the system can adjust to the matching problem.

The method is accurate on near-isometric shapes, where high resolution is typically preferred, and produces reasonable matches even with substantial non-isometric distortion. Experiments across both types of benchmark demonstrate superior performance. The findings support adaptive resolution as a way to retain accuracy for relatively compatible shapes while improving robustness when deformation makes correspondence more difficult.
neurips-2022-learning-multi-resolution-f.tldr: Spectral attention combines functional maps at multiple resolutions to make non-rigid shape matching more adaptive and robust.

paragraphs: Estimating a population mean becomes more complicated when data comes from users with different amounts and kinds of information. One user may contribute many observations while another contributes few, and their observations need not come from the same distribution. The paper treats both differences as central features of the problem.

The authors propose a simple model of heterogeneous user data and an estimator that preserves user-level differential privacy. The privacy requirement operates at the level of a user's contribution, while the statistical target remains the population-level mean. By allowing distributions and data quantities to vary together, the framework addresses a setting that cannot be captured by assuming every user samples identically.

The paper establishes asymptotic optimality of its estimator and proves general lower bounds on achievable error in the formulated problem. The lower bounds characterize fundamental limits, while asymptotic optimality describes the estimator's performance in the relevant limiting regime. Together, these results provide a theoretical account of accurate private mean estimation under the proposed heterogeneity model.
neurips-2022-mean-estimation-with-user-l.tldr: The paper develops an asymptotically optimal private mean estimator for a model where users differ in both data quantity and data distribution.

paragraphs: Cascading bandits model learning to rank from binary click feedback. The paper studies regret, which measures the cost of learning instead of already knowing the best ranking choices. For unstructured rewards, it establishes matching problem-independent upper and lower bounds, improving the best previously known bounds without relying on reward-gap parameters.

The key observation is that difficult instances have small click probabilities. For Bernoulli outcomes, a small mean also implies small variance. Confidence sets based on Bernstein and Chernoff bounds exploit that relationship and yield optimal algorithms up to logarithmic terms. Hoeffding-based algorithms instead have regret that is worse in its order of growth.

This difference is stronger than in standard non-cascading bandits, where accounting for variance improves only constants. The authors also introduce a variance-aware algorithm for structured linear rewards and prove a strict improvement over the prior regret bound. The results identify variance sensitivity as a central ingredient in optimal cascading-bandit learning, especially in the low-click regime highlighted by the analysis.
neurips-2022-minimax-regret-for-cascadin.tldr: Variance-aware confidence bounds yield optimal cascading-bandit regret up to logarithmic terms, with further improvements for linear rewards.

paragraphs: Cooperative agents may train together but need to act independently after deployment because communication is limited. Value-based methods address this by factorizing team value into individual components. The individual-global-max condition, or IGM, ensures that individual action choices agree with the optimal joint choice represented by that factorization.

QSCAN adds explicit sub-team coordination to this framework while preserving IGM. Its representation changes with sub-team size, spanning a spectrum from monotonic value functions to the full IGM function class. QMIX and QPLEX occupy the respective ends of that spectrum. This gives the framework flexibility to represent coordination at intermediate group sizes within a team.

Experiments report stronger performance than leading methods on matrix games, predator-prey tasks, and the MA-Gym Switch challenge. On selected StarCraft II micromanagement tasks, QSCAN achieves comparable performance. The evidence therefore supports gains on several tested coordination problems, alongside competitive results on the selected StarCraft tasks. The central contribution is a flexible way to represent sub-team interactions without abandoning the condition supporting decentralized decisions.
neurips-2022-multiagent-q-learning-with-.tldr: QSCAN represents coordination within sub-teams while preserving IGM, improving several tested cooperative tasks and matching competitors on selected StarCraft tasks.

paragraphs: Learning a controller for unknown nonlinear dynamics raises two connected questions: how to stabilize the system and how to certify that the learned controller does so. This paper tackles both by learning a neural controller together with a neural Lyapunov function. The function provides a certificate for a region of attraction of the controlled system.

The framework combines two neural networks with a satisfiability modulo theories solver. One network learns the unknown dynamics. The other identifies a candidate Lyapunov function and a stabilizing nonlinear controller. The solver then checks whether the candidate satisfies the required Lyapunov conditions, giving formal verification a specific role within the learning process.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees that, under mild assumptions, the resulting Lyapunov function also verifies for the unknown nonlinear system. This connection matters because the controller is developed using learned dynamics, yet the guarantee concerns the system being controlled. A few numerical experiments illustrate effectiveness. The stated certification applies to a region of attraction and remains conditional on the framework's assumptions.
neurips-2022-neural-lyapunov-control-of-.tldr: The framework learns unknown dynamics, a neural controller, and a Lyapunov certificate, providing regional stability guarantees under mild assumptions.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary models such as CLIP perform well across many classification tasks, but some tasks remain difficult in the zero-shot setting. This paper studies patching: improving those weak areas while preserving performance where the model already works adequately. The challenge is to make a targeted improvement without giving up the usefulness of the original model.

PAINT interpolates between the model's original weights and its weights after fine-tuning on a task needing improvement. On nine tasks with poor zero-shot CLIP performance, this approach raises accuracy by 15 to 60 percentage points while keeping ImageNet accuracy within one percentage point of the original. These results demonstrate the desired balance on the evaluated tasks.

The authors also show that one model can receive multiple patches and that results improve with model scale. In some cases, patching helps other tasks even when their classes do not overlap. Additional applications investigate counting and typographic attacks. Together, the findings show that task coverage can be expanded without retraining the model from scratch.
neurips-2022-patching-open-vocabulary-mo.tldr: PAINT mixes original and fine-tuned weights to improve weak CLIP tasks while largely preserving ImageNet accuracy in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Filtering language-model training data involves context-sensitive decisions about harmful, private, copyrighted, and other problematic material. The paper argues that existing ethical filtering approaches have often been ad hoc and insufficiently attentive to context. It proposes drawing on law, where governments have already developed rules for managing some of these inclusion and exclusion tradeoffs.

The authors release Pile of Law, an approximately 256GB and growing collection of open-source English legal and administrative text. It includes court opinions, contracts, administrative rules, and legislative records. They also distill legal norms governing toxic or private content into lessons for researchers and explain how those norms are reflected in the dataset.

A further contribution is the proposal to learn filtering rules directly from this legal data. The dataset therefore serves both as training material and as a resource for studying context-aware filtering. Pretraining on it may also support legal tasks with potential benefits for access to justice. Those downstream benefits and learned filtering possibilities are presented as opportunities, rather than established outcomes.
neurips-2022-pile-of-law-learning-respon.tldr: Pile of Law releases a large legal-text dataset and proposes using legal norms and data to guide context-sensitive training-data filtering.

paragraphs: Epistemic uncertainty concerns what a learner does not know. Measuring it requires more than producing a probability for an outcome: the learner must also represent uncertainty about its own predictive beliefs. This paper examines a proposed second-order approach in which predictions are distributions over probability distributions.

Ordinary first-order learners can be trained to predict accurate probabilities by minimizing suitable losses on observed examples. The authors investigate whether the same idea works for the second-order proposal. Their analysis shows that the proposed losses fail to give the learner an incentive to represent epistemic uncertainty faithfully. Optimizing those objectives therefore does not establish that the additional uncertainty information has the intended meaning.

The result separates expressive output structure from a training objective that supports its interpretation. A model may produce a distribution over distributions without being rewarded for accurately describing its lack of knowledge. The paper's criticism concerns the analyzed loss-based proposal and its objectives, exposing a problem in the connection between optimization and faithful epistemic uncertainty.
neurips-2022-pitfalls-of-epistemic-uncer.tldr: The analyzed losses for second-order predictors do not incentivize faithful representations of epistemic uncertainty.

paragraphs: A predictive system can sometimes hand a decision to a human expert or a larger model, but doing so incurs monetary or computational cost. Learning to defer aims to balance that cost against accuracy. This paper examines how training objectives shape both the base predictor and the decision to request expert help.

The authors identify two problems with existing losses: high deferral costs can encourage underfitting, and the deferral rule can depend too weakly on the base model's predictions. Their alternative trains the deferral function after the base model. Its objective is to request help when the base model's error probability exceeds the expert model's cost.

They interpret this procedure as using a partial surrogate for the ideal deferral loss, which can provide a tighter approximation and better performance. Benchmark experiments in learning to defer and adaptive inference support the effectiveness of the post-hoc scheme. The contribution ties the handoff decision more directly to the trained predictor's expected error and the price of obtaining expert assistance.
neurips-2022-post-hoc-estimators-for-lea.tldr: Training a deferral rule after the base model helps balance predicted error against expert cost and addresses weaknesses in existing losses.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces sets of possible answers with a target coverage level. This paper introduces MultiValid Prediction, or MVP, for sequential prediction on adversarial data. Its guarantees concern empirical coverage, allowing the method to address how often prediction sets contain the outcome over the sequence.

MVP strengthens overall marginal coverage in two ways. Coverage also holds conditional on the threshold used to turn a conformal score into a prediction set. In addition, users can specify a collection of feature-space subsets, including overlapping ones, and obtain coverage guarantees conditional on membership in each subset. This addresses distinctions that an overall coverage figure can conceal.

The method is computationally lightweight, with cost comparable to split conformal prediction. It does not require a held-out validation set, so all available data can be used to train the models supplying conformal scores. The paper provides theoretical results and extensive empirical evaluations. Its contribution combines these richer empirical coverage requirements with a practical sequential procedure.
neurips-2022-practical-adversarial-multi.tldr: MVP provides lightweight sequential prediction sets with empirical coverage guarantees across thresholds and specified groups, even on adversarial data.

paragraphs: Automatic differentiation makes it easy to combine model components, but the paper argues that learning algorithms remain constrained by having to express everything through backpropagation. The authors introduce Automatic Propagation to extend that flexibility to the learning procedure itself. Custom algorithms are packaged as propagators that perform their required computations and can be reused across computation graphs.

Proppo is a prototype implementation built on PyTorch's automatic differentiation framework. The authors demonstrate it with Monte Carlo gradient estimators, including reparameterization and likelihood-ratio gradients. They also implement total propagation and Gaussian shaping gradients, techniques previously used in model-based reinforcement learning that lacked publicly available implementations.

Minimal experiments show that these methods can improve gradient accuracy by orders of magnitude, particularly near the edge of chaos. The result is tied to those experimental settings. More broadly, the software contribution is a way to make specialized learning computations reusable and composable, giving algorithm designers a framework that extends beyond conventional automatic differentiation.
neurips-2022-proppo-a-message-passing-fr.tldr: Proppo generalizes automatic differentiation into reusable propagators for composing learning algorithms, demonstrated with specialized gradient estimators.

paragraphs: Low-light photography often trades noise against blur. Short exposures can produce noisy images, while long exposures can blur motion or camera shake. This paper pairs the two types of image so their complementary strengths can support restoration: short exposures are nearly free of blur, and long exposures have negligible noise.

The method learns deblurring and denoising collaboratively without requiring clean target images. Noisy short-exposure images provide supervision for deblurring. Sharp regions within the long-exposure images supply auxiliary supervision for denoising. Each task therefore receives useful information from an image degraded mainly in a different way, allowing the two restoration processes to benefit one another.

The paired input setting can be obtained with two cameras or synthesized from a long image burst. Experiments on synthetic and real-world images demonstrate effectiveness and practicality. The contribution is a self-supervised training arrangement that uses the different imperfections of the two exposures as complementary evidence, rather than depending on a single kind of degraded image.
neurips-2022-self-supervised-image-resto.tldr: Paired short and long exposures provide complementary supervision so denoising and deblurring can improve each other without clean targets.

paragraphs: Some molecular and material properties depend on electronic effects that extend beyond a local atomic neighborhood. Efficiently representing those effects is difficult, so machine learning models often neglect them. So3krates modifies attention to incorporate the geometry needed to describe relevant non-local quantum effects.

The model introduces spherical harmonic coordinates for each atom to represent higher-order geometric information. It separates that information from atomic features, allowing attention to operate on them independently. Spherical filters then support self-attention in this coordinate space. The authors show that this construction can describe non-local quantum effects over arbitrary length scales and find evidence that higher-order geometric correlations improve data efficiency and generalization.

On popular benchmarks, So3krates matches or exceeds leading performance while using 0.25 to 0.4 times the parameters of compared models. Reported speedups are 6 to 14 times for training and 2 to 11 times for inference. These results connect the physics-adapted representation to both predictive performance and computational efficiency in the evaluated comparisons.
neurips-2022-so3krates-equivariant-atten.tldr: So3krates uses spherical-coordinate attention to model non-local molecular effects, with strong benchmark performance and reported parameter and speed advantages.

paragraphs: A model can encounter test images from a distribution different from the one it learned during training. This paper studies test-time training, which adapts the model as each new input arrives. The adaptation uses self-supervision on that input, making the problem one of learning from a single test example.

The authors use masked autoencoders as the mechanism for this one-sample learning. The central choice is to make the incoming image itself provide a learning signal during prediction-time adaptation. This connects the model's adjustment to the particular example it must handle, rather than relying entirely on what was learned before encountering the changed distribution.

Experiments show improved generalization across many visual benchmarks involving distribution shifts. The paper also characterizes the improvement theoretically through the bias-variance trade-off, linking the observed benefit to a statistical account of adaptation. Together, the contributions present a simple self-supervised method and an explanation of its gains; the empirical claim concerns the evaluated visual shift benchmarks.
neurips-2022-test-time-training-with-mas.tldr: Masked autoencoders enable self-supervised adaptation to individual test images, improving reported robustness to visual distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Stabilized supralinear networks model cortical circuits with biological constraints that make training difficult. Strong connections between excitatory cells and expansive firing-rate nonlinearities can create unstable dynamics unless recurrent inhibition is appropriately tuned. This paper develops a training method that addresses those instabilities while retaining the features that motivate the model.

The method begins with a small network and gradually adds neurons during training through dynamics-neutral growth. The additions preserve the dynamics as network size increases, helping avoid the instability that complicates training. This provides a route beyond manually constructing these networks or training them under the restrictive conditions used in earlier work.

The authors demonstrate training on MNIST classification and on a more demanding inference task for natural image patches. The latter uses amortized Markov chain Monte Carlo inference under a Gaussian scale mixture model with diverse basis functions, which previous methods could not support. These demonstrations establish new training capabilities and open a path toward more scalable, computationally capable cortical-like networks.
neurips-2022-training-stochastic-stabili.tldr: Gradually growing stabilized supralinear networks without disturbing their dynamics enables training on classification and challenging natural-image inference.
